About Me

All you need to know about me

My name is Phemelo Mojalefa Rutlokoane, an Honours graduate in Biodiversity and Conservation Biology at the University of the Western Cape. I am a researcher interested in understanding how ecological patterns change across space, and how we can use data to explain those patterns. I enjoy working with spatial datasets, building reproducible workflows in R, and turning raw data into something that actually makes ecological sense.

Les Hyperion is where I document my work. I use it as both a portfolio and a working space to show projects in full, including methods, code, and interpretation.

Honours Project

My Honours research investigated the accuracy of hyperspectral imaging and LiDAR used during the BioSCape campaign in identifying Leucadendron argenteum_ populations across the Table Mountain National Park under the supervision of Dr. Patrick O'Farrell.

Figure 1: Random forests probability distribution map of Leucadendron argenteum.

I worked with high-resolution spectral datasets and field observations to test whether specific spectral regions correspond to vegetation structure and condition. I also learned to use Python for coding while working on my research project.

This project required:

  • Handling large raster datasets
  • Spectral region analysis
  • Integrating field and remote sensing data
  • Comparing machine learning models
  • Careful statistical interpretation

For me this project marked a shift from coursework to independent research. I designed the analysis framework, conducted the modelling, and interpreted the ecological implications.

Projects (Part of coursework)

1) Diel Vertical migration of Euphausia lucens at inshore and offshore stations in St Helena Bay, South Africa

In this project, I analysed the vertical migration of Antarctic krill (Euphausia lucens) using quantitative analyses. The aim was to investigate environmental drivers of the vertical distribution of the krill and explore how the spatial structure influences abundance estimates.

Figure 2: Weighted Mean Depth (WMD) plot of all E. lucens life stages at both inshore and offshore stations.

I focused on data cleaning, spatial interpolation, and modelling relationships between krill density and environmental variables. The dataset was originally collected and compiled by my professor, and my role was to conduct the analysis and interpret the spatial patterns.

This project strengthened my ability to:

  • Work with large ecological datasets
  • Conduct spatial modelling in R
  • Interpret marine ecological patterns critically

Data provided by: [Prof. Mark Gibbons].

2) Using multivariate environmental variables to quantify the distributions of Adder populations in South Africa

This was a collaborative class project focused on modelling the distribution of the Adder species across South Africa. The goal was to explore how environmental gradients shape the distribution and community composition of Adder species.

Figure 3: Distribution of B. gabonica, B. cornuta, B. caudalis and B. inornata over the change in elevation across South Africa with B. gabonica restricted in the Coastal Indian Ocean Belt in Kwa-Zulu Natal.

We built species distribution models, ran multivariate analyses and evaluated how land cover, elevation, and bioclimatic variables influenced the distribution of Adders.

Figure 4: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) biplot of environmental variables across South African biomes.

This project was completed in collaboration with my classmates, who contributed to data preparation, modelling, and interpretation. It introduced me to species distribution modelling workflows and strengthened my understanding of spatial ecology in terrestrial systems.

Completed with: [Kezia Samuels] and [Shane Ngwenya].

What I am building

I am still early in my research career. I do not yet have any publication list (I am working on submitting a publication on my Honours project) – but I have strong technical foundations, growing research independence, and a clear direction of where I want to be in life.

I want to work at the interface of field ecology and spatial modelling. I am interested in disturbance ecology, fire regimes, ocean climate, invasive species and remote sensing applications.

Les Hyperion will grow as I grow. It will document not only my finished projects, but also ideas, methods, and analytical notes
